title: Craft Room Wall Storage: Pegboard, Shelves, Door Racks and Pocket Organizers That Free Up Your Table
seoTitle: Craft Room Wall Storage Ideas That Free Your Table
excerpt: Craft room wall storage ideas: plan the wall in reach zones, use pegboard for daily tools, shelves for bins and paper, the door for small supplies and clear boxes for beads, with heavy items low.
imageCaption: Stacks of clear rectangular and square plastic boxes, one open with beads and one with earrings. Photo: Sesoris product catalog.
content: The best **craft room wall storage** moves supplies off the table and onto vertical space you can see at a glance. Start with a pegboard or rail system above the work surface for the tools you use every session, add shelves higher up for bins and paper, use pocket organizers and the back of the door for small supplies, and keep tiny parts in labeled clear boxes. Put heavy items low, anchor anything tall to the wall and leave the area right above your work surface for daily tools only.

In most craft rooms, the floor and the table fill up first. Fabric, paper, paint, yarn and tools spread across every flat surface until there is no room left to make anything. The walls, meanwhile, often hold nothing but a calendar. This guide walks through how to plan craft room wall storage, which systems suit which supplies, and how to keep a wall full of supplies looking organized rather than chaotic.
## Why Wall Storage Works in a Craft Room
Craft supplies are mostly small, colorful and used in combinations. That makes them a good fit for walls, for three reasons.

- **You can see everything.** When supplies hang or sit at eye level, you notice what you have before you buy more.
- **The work surface stays clear.** Tools on the wall above the table are within reach but not in the way.
- **It uses space you already have.** A small spare room or corner often has more wall area than floor area.
Wall storage does not replace closed storage entirely. Fabric, paper and anything that fades in light still need bins or cabinets. But a well-planned wall takes pressure off the table and the floor.
## Plan the Wall in Zones
Before you hang anything, look at the wall as a set of zones based on reach and use.

- **Above the work surface (the reach zone):** the tools and supplies you use in almost every session, such as scissors, rulers, tape, glue and pens.
- **Eye level to just above head height:** supplies you use often but not always, such as paint, markers, ribbon and current project bins.
- **High shelves:** backstock, seasonal supplies and finished projects, in labeled bins with handles.
- **Low wall and floor level:** heavy items such as paper reams, large paint containers and machines when not in use.

Sketch the wall on paper with measurements, mark outlets, light switches and windows, and decide which zone each type of supply belongs in. Our [craft storage room planning guide](/blog/craft-storage-room) covers the full room layout.
## Craft Room Wall Storage Options Compared

| Wall system | Best for | Strengths | Limits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pegboard with hooks and baskets | Tools, tape, ribbon spools, small bins | Very flexible, easy to rearrange | Hooks can lift out if not secured |
| Wall shelves | Bins, jars, paper trays, books | Hold more weight and bulk | Need secure mounting into studs or proper anchors |
| Rail with hanging cups or hooks | Pens, brushes, scissors | Slim, fits above a desk | Holds only light items |
| Fabric pocket organizer | Small supplies, patterns, notions | Soft, no drilling with a hook or nail | Pockets sag if overloaded |
| Over-the-door rack or pockets | Paint bottles, glue, small boxes | Uses the back of the door | Door must still close freely |
| Freestanding shelf against the wall | Bins and boxes | No drilling, can move | Tall units should be anchored |
Most craft rooms use two or three of these together: a pegboard or rail above the table, shelves higher up, and the door for overflow.
## Pegboard: The Most Flexible Option
Pegboard is popular in craft rooms because you can move hooks, cups and shelves as your hobbies change. A single panel above the work table can hold most daily tools.

- **Hang tools by type:** cutting tools together, measuring tools together, adhesives together.
- **Use small baskets or cups** for pens, brushes and markers.
- **Hang ribbon or washi tape** on a dowel or a straight hook.
- **Secure hooks** with clips or locks so they do not come off when you lift a tool.
- **Outline tools** with a marker or tape if you want everyone to return things to the right spot.

Leave some empty hooks for new tools and projects. A full pegboard looks busy and makes it harder to find things. Our [pegboard organization guide](/blog/pegboard-garage-organization) is written for garages, but the layout and hook tips work just as well in a craft room.
## Shelves for Bins, Jars and Paper
Shelves handle bulkier supplies that pegboard cannot, such as bins of yarn, jars of buttons and stacks of paper.

- **Use matching bins** so a full shelf still looks calm.
- **Label every bin** on the front with large, clear text.
- **Store paper flat** in trays, or upright in magazine files, to stop it curling.
- **Keep jars and clear containers** for small, colorful items you like to see.
- **Put heavier bins on lower shelves.**

Mount wall shelves into studs or with anchors rated for the load, following the manufacturer's instructions. If you prefer not to drill, a freestanding shelf against the wall works, but tall units should still be secured. Health Canada advises using anti-tip devices such as angle braces or safety straps to anchor furniture to the wall, placing heavier items in lower drawers so furniture does not become top-heavy, and removing toys or attractive items from the top of furniture so children are not tempted to climb ([Health Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/household-products/furniture-appliance-television-tip-overs.html)).
Our [wall shelf storage ideas](/blog/wall-shelf-storage-ideas-transform-home-organization-2026) and [floating shelf ideas](/blog/floating-shelf-ideas) cover more shelf styles.
## Use the Back of the Door
The back of a craft room door is one of the most overlooked storage spaces. It is ideal for small items you want to see.
![A black eight-tier over-the-door rack with wire baskets and door hooks, shown empty on a white background. Photo: Sesoris product catalog](/images/blog/craft-room-wall-storage-door-rack.webp)

An over-the-door rack with shallow baskets keeps paint bottles, glue, small boxes and spools in view. The [8-tier over-the-door organizer](/product/over-the-door-pantry-organizer-8-tier) has eight wire baskets, each 16 inches wide and 4.9 inches deep, with adjustable spacing. It hangs on doors up to 2 inches thick, needs at least 7.1 inches of clearance behind the door, and can also be fixed to a wall with the included screws. The supplier rates it at 26.5 pounds total and 3.31 pounds per basket, so it suits paint, glue and small supplies rather than heavy tools.
![An empty white over-the-door organizer with 24 clear pockets hanging from three metal hooks. Photo: Sesoris product catalog](/images/blog/craft-room-wall-storage-door-pockets.webp)

Clear pockets are another option for soft or flat supplies. The [over-the-door organizer with 24 clear pockets](/product/over-the-door-shoe-organizer-24-pocket) is sold for shoes, but the listing notes the pockets also hold small items such as rolled towels, toys, makeup or cleaning supplies. Each pocket measures 7.87 x 4.25 inches, so it fits thread, small skeins, paint pens, stencils or packs of embellishments. It hangs from three included hooks with no tools.
## Fabric Pocket Organizers for Small Supplies
Not every wall needs drilling. Fabric pocket organizers hang from a nail or hook and keep small supplies at hand.

![A yellow fabric three-pocket wall organizer hanging from a wooden rod, with a plush toy and glasses in the pockets. Photo: Sesoris product catalog](/images/blog/craft-room-wall-storage-wall-pockets.webp)

The [hanging wall organizer with 3 pockets](/product/hanging-wall-organizer-3-pocket-yellow) measures 7.87 x 24 inches, with three pockets about 7.1 inches wide, 5.5 inches tall and 3.1 inches deep. The fabric is stiff linen-cotton, so the pockets keep their shape, and it hangs from a rope loop on a nail or hook. Beside a sewing machine, it can hold a seam ripper, pins and a measuring tape. Next to a drawing desk, it can hold sketchbooks and pencils.
## Clear Boxes for Beads, Charms and Tiny Parts
Beads, sequins, buttons and jewelry findings are hard to store on open walls because they spill. Small lidded boxes on a shelf or in a wall-mounted tray keep them contained.
![Open clear plastic boxes holding colorful resin charms, pearls and small gold findings. Photo: Sesoris product catalog](/images/blog/craft-room-wall-storage-clear-boxes.webp)

The [clear plastic storage boxes, 24 pack](/product/clear-plastic-storage-boxes-24-pack) include 12 rectangular boxes measuring 5.11 x 3.14 x 1.18 inches and 12 square boxes measuring 2.16 x 2.16 x 0.78 inches. Each has a hinged lid with a snap closure, so beads and findings stay put if a box tips over. Stack them on a shelf with labels facing out, or line them up in a shallow tray so you can see every color at once.
## Wall Storage by Craft Type
Different crafts need different wall setups.

- **Sewing:** pegboard or rail for scissors, rulers and rotary cutters, thread on a spool rack, and fabric folded in bins on shelves away from direct sun.
- **Paper crafts and scrapbooking:** paper stored flat or upright in labeled files, punches and stamps on shelves, and tools on a rail above the table.
- **Painting and drawing:** brushes upright in cups on a rail, paint bottles on door baskets or shallow shelves, and paper in flat trays.
- **Knitting and crochet:** yarn in cubbies or open bins on shelves, hooks and needles in cups, and patterns in a pocket organizer. Our [yarn storage ideas](/blog/yarn-storage-ideas) have more detail.
- **Jewelry making:** clear boxes for beads and findings on a shelf, and pliers and wire cutters on pegboard.
## Keep a Full Wall Looking Calm
A wall full of supplies can look cluttered if it lacks structure. A few design choices keep it calm.

- **Limit containers to one or two styles** and colors.
- **Group by color within categories**, such as paints or threads, which looks good and is easy to scan.
- **Leave some empty space** on each shelf and panel.
- **Use one label style** across the whole wall.
- **Hide less attractive items** in closed bins on higher shelves.
## Wall Storage for a Small or Shared Craft Space

Not every crafter has a whole room. Many work from a corner of a spare bedroom, a guest room or the dining room. Wall storage matters even more in these spaces, because it keeps supplies contained in one area instead of spreading through the house.

- **Claim one wall section** and keep every craft supply within it, so the rest of the room stays clear.
- **Choose closable storage up high** in shared rooms, such as lidded bins or a cabinet, so the wall looks tidy when guests stay.
- **Mount a fold-down or narrow table** below the wall storage if floor space is tight, and keep only a small tool rail above it.
- **Use the door of a nearby closet** for overflow supplies rather than adding more to the wall.
- **Keep a portable caddy** for the supplies of your current project, so you can carry them to a bigger table and back.

In a guest room, a curtain or a pair of panels on a ceiling track can hide an entire wall of shelves when the room is in use. That way the wall works as craft storage most of the year and disappears when it needs to.
## Light the Wall So You Can Find Things
A wall of supplies is only useful if you can see it. Overhead lighting often leaves shelves and pegboard in shadow, especially the lower zones.

- **Add a lamp or task light** over the work surface so the reach zone is bright.
- **Consider plug-in or battery strip lights** under shelves to light bins below.
- **Keep fabric and paper out of direct sun**, which can fade colors over time.
Good light also makes color-matching easier, which matters for painting, quilting and paper crafts.
## Rotate Supplies With Your Projects

Wall storage works best when it reflects what you are working on now. Supplies for a finished project or a hobby you have paused can move to higher shelves or closed bins, freeing the reach zone for current work. When you start something new, bring its supplies down to eye level. This simple rotation keeps the most valuable wall space for the things you need today.
## Declutter Before You Hang Anything
Wall storage works best when it holds what you actually use. Before setting it up, go through your supplies.

1. **Sort by craft and by type.**
2. **Remove dried-out paint, broken tools and supplies for crafts you no longer do.**
3. **Decide how much of each supply you need** for current and next projects.
4. **Donate extras** to schools, community centers or other crafters.

Our [craft room organization guide](/blog/craft-room-organization) walks through the full declutter and setup process, and our [craft closet organization ideas](/blog/craft-closet-organization-ideas-transform-creative-space-2026) help if your supplies live in a closet rather than a room.
## Safety and Practical Tips

- **Find studs** before mounting heavy shelves or pegboard, or use anchors rated for the load.
- **Anchor tall freestanding units** to the wall with braces or straps.
- **Keep heavy items low** and light items up high.
- **Store sharp tools** where children cannot reach them, with blades covered.
- **Keep paints and solvents** in their original containers with lids closed.
- **Leave clearance** around outlets and switches.
## Maintenance Routine

- **After each session:** return tools to the wall and put lids back on containers.
- **Monthly:** check labels, refill or reorder supplies and move finished projects off the wall.
- **Twice a year:** review everything, remove what you no longer use and rearrange the wall for current projects.

If you are furnishing the room from scratch, our [craft room storage furniture guide](/blog/craft-room-storage-furniture-complete-review-buying-guide-2026) compares cabinets, carts and tables, and our [craft storage room ideas](/blog/craft-storage-room-ideas-transform-creative-space-smart-organization-2026) offer more layouts.
## Frequently Asked Questions
**Q: What is the best wall storage for a craft room?**
A combination works best: pegboard or a rail above the work surface for daily tools, shelves higher up for bins and paper, and the back of the door for small supplies.
**Q: How do I store craft supplies on the wall without drilling?**
Use fabric pocket organizers on a nail or hook, over-the-door racks or pocket organizers, and freestanding shelves against the wall, anchored if they are tall.
**Q: Where should heavy craft supplies go?**
On lower shelves or the floor. Health Canada advises placing heavier items low so furniture does not become top-heavy, and anchoring furniture to the wall.
**Q: How do I organize small craft supplies like beads?**
Store them in small clear boxes with snap lids, labeled on the front, on a shelf or in a shallow tray where you can see every color.
**Q: Is pegboard good for a craft room?**
Yes. Pegboard is flexible and easy to rearrange, so it suits tools, tape, ribbon and small baskets. Secure the hooks so they do not lift out.
**Q: How do I keep a craft wall from looking cluttered?**
Use one or two container styles, group items by color within categories, use one label style and leave some empty space on every shelf.
**Q: Can I use an over-the-door shoe organizer for crafts?**
Yes. Clear pockets work well for thread, paint pens, stencils, small skeins and packs of embellishments, as long as items fit the pocket size.
**Q: How often should I reorganize craft room wall storage?**
Return tools after every session, do a short check monthly and review the whole wall twice a year.
## Final Thoughts

Craft room wall storage frees the table and floor by putting supplies where you can see them. Plan the wall in zones, use pegboard or a rail for daily tools, shelves for bins and paper and the door for small supplies, and keep tiny parts in labeled clear boxes. Put heavy items low, anchor tall furniture and declutter before you hang anything. With a quick reset after each session, the wall stays as useful as the day you set it up.
